articles.title: Phase-homogeneous mixed halide perovskites for stable tandem photovoltaics
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10929-2Phase-homogeneous mixed halide perovskites for stable tandem photovoltaics
articles.content: Mixed-halide wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskites needed in tandem photovoltaics suffer from phase segregation, even at the time of initial film formation – the result of asymmetric nucleation of I-rich and Br-rich phases1-3. Known homogenization strategies tune Pb2+ coordination strength4-6; however, Pb2+-based modulation applies across all Pb2+ centers and does not preferentially address the problem that PbBr x nucleates faster than does PbI x . Here we introduce a selective coordination principle: we tune local Lewis-base hardness at the donor atom through a molecular dipole, an approach that constrains the polarizability of the O-donor’s outermost electrons. The harder O-donor preferentially coordinates the harder Pb2+ of PbBr x , selectively retarding Br-rich nucleation and synchronizing it with PbI x . This leads to compositionally homogeneous WBG films, enabling solar cells with bandgaps of 1.62 eV, 1.68 eV, and 1.88 eV, each achieving enhanced PCE and extended stability (1500 h, ≥T 90 , 1 sun and 65 °C). Perovskite/organic tandem cells fabricated with these WBG films and an infrared-active organic cell deliver certified 27.0% (steady-state 26.4%) efficiency, with T 91 (ISOS-L2 at 65 °C) of 1000 h.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in perovskite solar cell technology, achieving stable, high-efficiency tandem photovoltaics with improved material homogeneity and extended operational stability. This advancement has broad implications for renewable energy generation and climate action by potentially enabling more efficient and durable solar panels for widespread use.

articles.personality_presentation:

They used a special chemical trick to control how parts of the material come together during production. This method slows down the formation of one part of the material so it matches the other, creating a balanced and stable film. Using this improved film, they built tandem solar cells that reached over 27% efficiency and stayed stable for more than 1,000 hours under heat and sunlight.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it solves the problem of instability and unevenness in a key solar cell material. By making the material more uniform and stable, the solar cells can work better and last longer. This means solar panels could become more reliable and efficient, helping to produce cleaner energy more effectively.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely work on scaling up this method to produce solar panels on a larger scale. They may also explore combining this approach with other improvements to make even better and longer-lasting solar cells.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new chemical technique creates more stable and efficient solar cell materials, pushing tandem solar cells closer to practical, long-lasting use.

articles.title: Is it time to stop using glue and labels on paper?
articles.summary: Labels and adhesives can prevent paper from being recycled but there's new tech aimed at changing that.
articles.content:
But what if you could skip the adhesive altogether?

That's the idea that three firms from Germany - Fraunhofer, Hermann Ultraschall, and Henkel - have come up with.

It's no coincidence they are all German, as the country is known for its Packaging Valley, external, a hub for the packaging industry.

Their efforts to innovate are partly a bid to satisfy ever tightening regulation around commercial recycling, and rising fines for those who fall foul.

With that in mind, German research organisation Fraunhofer established the PAPURE project in 2023 to develop a laser-based heating process that can seal paper packaging without an adhesive at all.

From September, when the project is set to officially close, Fraunhofer hopes to find an industry partner to take the technology to market. Fraunhofer researchers exhibited their work at the Interpack packaging trade show in Dusseldorf in May, and are hopeful that the interest they attracted will come to fruition.

"There are not really many paper sealing technologies without any foreign materials, so it's a great technology and we feel it's likely that we can bring it to market," says researcher group leader Fabian Kayatz.

"If we are optimistic, we will have the first solution out in two years."

Also in 2023, engineering firm Hermann Ultraschall bought the rights to develop a patented ultrasonic paper sealing technology, a process which it likens to welding.

"We are really actively at the moment in discussion with several really big players in the market with the focus of bringing this technology into mass production," says Michael Baumann, the company's head of business development packaging.

"One customer told me this is an innovation they have never seen before."

Yet these seemingly simple solutions stem from complex technology, so naturally, there are challenges.

Firstly, it's not as simple as simply getting product manufacturers and packaging companies to swap out their old packaging for these new options. It requires updating, and in some cases, completely replacing, existing machinery, which can be costly and time consuming.

"The packaging industry has existing machines which are all designed for glue materials. Some kind of redesign is probably necessary, and this is our biggest challenge," says Hermann Ultraschall's Baumann.

Yet Volker Franke, also a research group leader at Fraunhofer, is confident that those existing machines can be modified by integrating the laser module that PAPURE has been developing.

They both acknowledge that the production rate is also currently much slower than that for paper packaging that uses adhesives, but Franke says a key benefit PAPURE is selling is fully automated production, which he believes can continue to be developed for speed.

The other issue is that the technologies don't work on all types of paper.

"It's not possible to bond every paper material," Baumann confirms. "But we are actively in discussion with paper manufacturers about how they can produce a raw material in a way that makes it easy to bond."

PAPURE has also yet to find a way to apply their laser sealing technology to food-grade packaging, which needs a coating to protect the item. This tends to be why plastic is often favoured for packaging food.

But this is something Henkel, with both a consumer brand division, and adhesive technologies division, has cracked.

In February, Henkel announced the launch of the first cold seal solution that works with barrier coated paper, which is both recyclable and suitable for food products.

Barrier paper can be a difficult surface to bond, and using heat isn't suitable for heat sensitive food products like ice cream or chocolate. Hence the cold seal solution, in which enough pressure is applied for the barrier coated paper to be bonded against itself.

articles.title: Why budding birders are flocking to Shazam-like apps to identify avians
articles.summary: Birdwatchers tell the BBC how apps have changed their lifelong hobby - and attracted new birders.
articles.content:
Megan Szostak, 26, was always a "bird kid".

The urge to watch and appreciate the world around her - and avians flitting in and out of it - has been ingrained in her since childhood, when she was given her grandfather's binoculars after he died.

Armed with this and a field guide in her home of San Francisco, she set about identifying birds from an early age.

But in recent years, her birding toolbelt has expanded to include something far more modern - an app.

"I had friends who probably wouldn't describe themselves as birders, but more just curious about nature and the world around them, recommend it to me," Megan said.

She is one of many millions of people who have downloaded Merlin Bird ID, which claims to be able to identify almost any bird by its look, song or call.

"I think that it's been a really great tool that I've integrated into my birding routine," she said.

And whether down to heatwaves sending more people outdoors, or younger people delving into birding, these apps are booming in popularity.

Chief among them is Merlin Bird ID, which was developed by Cornell University's Lab of Ornithology.

It has been downloaded 12 million times in 2026 alone, according to director Jessie Barry - who says it has had 42 million downloads overall.

She says the app has come a long way since it first launched in the US in 2014, with machine learning systems which could identify 285 common bird species from photos.

A real feather in its cap at the time, but a decade or so on, and it can now identify 11,000 species of birds - around as many as exist in the world.

Barry put the development down to AI, as well as "an amazing community of global bird watchers who are able to submit their recordings" - meaning more data to train the tech.

The app's significant user base and technological advancement demonstrate a meaningful positive impact on public engagement with wildlife and conservation.

articles.title: The prehistoric species fighting for survival in Lough Neagh
articles.summary: Restrictions have been placed on fishing the critically-endangered European eel in Lough Neagh to try to restore the species
articles.content:
The Lough Neagh eel was the first Northern Ireland product to be granted Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status by the EU.

But no yellow eels will be caught on the Lough this year - or for the next two years - following the closure of the fishery.

Only a minimal amount (25 tonnes) of silver eels (fully mature) may be caught at the Lough Neagh Fishermen's Co-operative.

People who depend on eel fishing for the bulk of their income are now waiting to hear what support they may get from Stormont.

They point the finger firmly at environmental pressures in the Lough.

With eel-fishing bans already in place in some countries, some scientists say the writing has been on the wall for decades.

Daera has said a financial assistance scheme has been developed and the "necessary approvals for the proposal are currently being pursued".
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant conservation efforts to protect the critically endangered European eel in Lough Neagh by imposing fishing restrictions, which has broad environmental and ecological significance. It highlights a meaningful policy action aimed at species recovery and ecosystem preservation, with tangible impact on biodiversity and local communities.
articles.personality_title: Fishing limits set to protect endangered European eels in Lough Neagh
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The European eel is a species that has been living for thousands of years but is now critically endangered. Lough Neagh, a large lake in Northern Ireland, is an important place for these eels. The eel from this lake was the first product in Northern Ireland to receive special protection from the European Union, called Protected Geographical Indication (PGI).

**What happened** – To help the European eel population recover, authorities have stopped all fishing of young yellow eels in Lough Neagh for the next three years. Only a small amount of mature silver eels can be caught by the local fishermen's cooperative. This decision started recently and aims to reduce pressure on the eel population.

**Impact** – These fishing restrictions are important because the European eel has been declining for many years due to environmental changes and overfishing. Protecting the eels in Lough Neagh helps keep the lake’s ecosystem balanced and supports the survival of this ancient species. At the same time, local fishermen, who rely on eel fishing for their income, are waiting to see what financial support the government will provide during this period.

**What's next step** – The Northern Ireland government department responsible, DAERA, is working on a financial assistance plan to help fishermen during the fishing ban. They are currently seeking approval to put this plan into action. Scientists and policymakers will continue to monitor the eel population to decide when fishing can safely resume.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New fishing limits in Lough Neagh aim to protect the endangered European eel while balancing the needs of local fishing communities.

**Contexto** – La anguila europea es una especie que ha existido durante miles de años, pero ahora está en peligro crítico de extinción. Lough Neagh, un gran lago en Irlanda del Norte, es un lugar importante para estas anguilas. La anguila de este lago fue el primer producto de Irlanda del Norte en recibir una protección especial de la Unión Europea llamada Indicación Geográfica Protegida (IGP).

**Qué pasó** – Para ayudar a que la población de anguilas europeas se recupere, las autoridades han prohibido la pesca de anguilas jóvenes llamadas anguilas amarillas en Lough Neagh durante los próximos tres años. Solo se permite capturar una pequeña cantidad de anguilas maduras llamadas anguilas plateadas, y esto solo por la cooperativa local de pescadores. Esta medida comenzó recientemente para reducir la presión sobre la población de anguilas.

**Impacto** – Estas restricciones de pesca son importantes porque la población de anguilas europeas ha disminuido durante muchos años debido a cambios en el medio ambiente y a la sobrepesca. Proteger a las anguilas en Lough Neagh ayuda a mantener el equilibrio del ecosistema del lago y apoya la supervivencia de esta especie antigua. Al mismo tiempo, los pescadores locales, que dependen de la pesca de anguilas para su ingreso, esperan saber qué apoyo financiero les dará el gobierno.

**Próximo paso** – El departamento del gobierno de Irlanda del Norte responsable, DAERA, está trabajando en un plan de ayuda financiera para apoyar a los pescadores durante la prohibición de pesca. Actualmente están buscando la aprobación para poner este plan en marcha. Científicos y responsables políticos continuarán monitoreando la población de anguilas para decidir cuándo se podrá reanudar la pesca de forma segura.

**Resumen en una frase** – Nuevos límites de pesca en Lough Neagh buscan proteger a la anguila europea en peligro mientras se equilibra el bienestar de las comunidades pesqueras locales.
